stats.fact: MiniMax-M2.1 is listed by MiniMax as a 230B-parameter model with 10B activated per inference, optimized for code generation, refactoring, polyglot code, precision refactoring, and enhanced reasoning.
MiniMax's API docs list MiniMax-M2.1 with a 204,800-token context window and approximately 60 tokens per second output speed; MiniMax-M2.1-highspeed is listed at approximately 100 tokens per second.
MiniMax says M2.1 model weights are open-source and available for local deployment on Hugging Face, with API access available through the MiniMax Open Platform.
The official MiniMax-M2.1 GitHub repository recommends SGLang, vLLM, Transformers, MLX-LM, and KTransformers as serving options for local deployment.
MiniMax recommends inference parameters temperature=1.0, top_p=0.95, and top_k=40 for MiniMax-M2.1.
MiniMax reports M2.1 scores of 74.0 on SWE-bench Verified, 49.4 on Multi-SWE-bench, 72.5 on SWE-bench Multilingual, and 47.9 on Terminal-bench 2.0.
MiniMax reports M2.1 VIBE benchmark scores of 88.6 average, 91.5 for Web, 89.7 for Android, 88.0 for iOS, 87.1 for Simulation, and 86.7 for Backend.
MiniMax reports M2.1 tool and browsing scores of 43.5 on Toolathlon, 47.4 on BrowseComp, and 62.0 on BrowseComp with context management.

MiniMax pay-as-you-go pricing lists MiniMax-M2.1 at $0.30 per million input tokens and $1.20 per million output tokens, with prompt cache read at $0.03 per million tokens and prompt cache write at $0.375 per million tokens.
MiniMax-M2.1 is now categorized under legacy models in MiniMax pay-as-you-go pricing, while newer M-series options including M2.5, M2.7, and M3 are available.
MiniMax exposes OpenAI-compatible and Anthropic-compatible protocols for coding tools that support custom base URLs.

MiniMax's current model list includes M3 with a 1M context window and newer M2.7/M2.5 variants, so an M2.1 guide should present M2.1 as a strong open-weight coding model rather than the newest MiniMax model.

angles: M2.1 is the practical bridge between open weights and agentic coding: strong enough for SWE-bench-style work, deployable locally, and callable through hosted APIs.
The headline is not just parameter count: 230B total with 10B active means developers get large-model breadth with sparse-inference economics.
M2.1's polyglot pitch matters because production systems rarely stay in Python; emphasize Java, Go, Rust, C++, TypeScript, JavaScript, Kotlin, and Python workflows.
The guide should compare three deployment paths: native MiniMax API for fastest setup, third-party aggregators for tool compatibility, and local serving for privacy/control.
Use VIBE as a differentiator for full-stack app generation, but explicitly label it as a first-party benchmark that needs external validation.
M2.1 is no longer the latest MiniMax coding model by June 2026, so frame it as a legacy but still relevant open-weight option for teams that value self-hosting and stable cost.
Highspeed variant and cache pricing deserve a production section because agent loops can become output-heavy and repeated-context-heavy quickly.
Tool-calling and Anthropic/OpenAI-compatible endpoints make M2.1 interesting for existing Cline, Kilo, RooCode, OpenHands, LangChain, and custom agent stacks.

source_notes: Prioritize MiniMax official docs, Hugging Face, and GitHub for factual specs because third-party model pages disagree on exact context, output, and provider pricing.
Mention that MiniMax's pricing docs place M2.1 under legacy models as of June 30, 2026.
Do not overstate VIBE as an industry-standard benchmark; describe it as MiniMax's full-stack application benchmark using Agent-as-a-Verifier.
For local deployment, avoid promising laptop-friendly inference without quantization/hardware caveats because the official model is 230B total parameters.
